IMPACT ANALYSES OF NEW INSTITUTIONS
For several years, under grants from NSF/RANN, The Futures Group has been
conducting a series of policy analyses and impact assessments of new
institutional arrangements: legalized gambling in the form of lotteries
and off-track betting, prepaid legal services, and currently, unionization
of state court employees. These studies have been designed to be of 1mme-
diate practical use to decision makers in state and local governments,
professional groups, unions, and business.
Legalized Gambling
The study of lotteries and off-track betting
(The Impact of Legalized
Gambling, Praeger Publishers) has been accepted as the basic text in the
field.  It furnishes information on the history, operations, financial
returns, and economic and societal impacts. of these recently spreading
forms of legalized gambling, and defines policy issues for legislators
and the public. It also analyzes differences in impact between existing
and proposed forms of legalized gambling. The weekly lottery, for instance,
is probably the least harmful form of public gambling; it is least likely
to encourage heavy betting because it is a non-multiplier game (the prize
is not dependent on how much one bets) and has a low bettor involvement in
terms of skill and entertainment, a long payout interval, and low incentive
to re-bet winnings.
Casino gambling, on the other hand, has exactly oppo-
site attributes.
Prepaid Legal Services
Prepaid legal services have recently emerged as a possible fringe
benefit for workers. The Futures Group study (Prepaid Legal Services
Lexington Books) analyzes experience in the field to date, identifies
potential future impacts on the legal profession, on the courts, on plan
members, and on the public, and points out how impacts might differ under
alternative forms of the plans. "Open" plans put no general limitation
on the opportunity for any lawyer to represent members, operating in a
similar manner to Blue Shield-type medical plans, while "closed" plans
limit in some way the number of lawyers who may provide services, either
through a selected panel or a hired staff of lawyers. Unions have generally
leaned in the direction of closed plans, while bar associations in a number
of states have established open plans.  It appears that, assuming a rate of
growth comparable to other fringe benefits, the overall impact on employ-
ment in the legal profession would not be massive, although sizable numbers
could be involved (5 to 10 percent of al1 lawyers by 1985)
